Chapter 1: How Racial Trauma Lives in the Body
When we think about racism, it's easy to picture it as something that happens out there—maybe a heated argument, a headline that stings, or a policy that shapes lives from a distance.
But for so many people, the real impact of racism hits much closer to home. It settles deep inside, woven right into the body itself.
Let me paint you a picture. Imagine a child tensing up when their parent’s voice suddenly sharpens. Or think about a teenager whose heart races after a tough moment at school. These might seem like everyday reactions, but really, it’s the body’s way of holding on to pain, fear, and uncertainty—sometimes for years, and sometimes, believe it or not, across generations.
One memory comes to mind—a young boy sitting at his grandmother’s kitchen table, watching her knead dough. Her hands are strong, worn by years of work and worry. She hums quietly, but her eyes carry a kind of heaviness. The boy doesn’t know the full story, but he feels something in her movements—a gentle caution, almost like she’s always ready to flinch.
Later on, he learns that his grandmother grew up in a world where safety was never promised. Just a knock at the door could spell trouble. Her body learned to brace for it, and that lesson didn’t just live in her stories—it lingered in her muscles, her bones, even in the way she moved.
Most people don’t realize that trauma isn’t just a memory or a feeling. It’s physical. It gets stored in the nervous system, almost like the body is building its own history book. When we sense a threat—real or imagined—our bodies respond: muscles tighten, breathing shifts, hearts pound. And if those threats never let up, if they’re just always lurking, the body adapts. It stays on high alert, ready for anything.
This is especially true for anyone living with the daily stress of racism. Their bodies start to expect danger—even when nothing’s actually happening. It’s exhausting, and it’s tough to shake.
But here’s something worth thinking about: trauma doesn’t just stop with one person. It ripples out. A parent who grew up afraid might become super protective, teaching their kids to always be careful. A teacher, shaped by their own hurts, might react with suspicion or impatience. Even people who haven’t faced racism directly can feel its weight—maybe as guilt, maybe as anxiety, or just as a vague unease they can’t quite name.
The body’s response to trauma is something we all share, but the reasons behind that trauma? Those are very different. In America, the legacies of slavery, segregation, and violence have left deep scars—especially on Black bodies. But white bodies carry their own burdens too, often unspoken or denied. Think of police officers, caught between duty and fear, developing patterns of tension and vigilance. Every group holds pain in its own way. But the result? A society where so many bodies are bracing, always waiting for the next blow.
So, how do we start to heal? It all begins with noticing. Most of us rush through our days, ignoring that tightness in our shoulders or the knot in our stomach. But when we pause—just for a moment—and really notice what our bodies are telling us, we start to see how deeply trauma shapes our lives. Sometimes, just taking a breath or sitting still can bring up old wounds. It’s not easy; sometimes the pain feels way too big or too old to face. But every act of noticing, no matter how small, is a step toward healing.
And here’s something powerful: healing isn’t just a solo journey. When one person starts to heal, it opens a door for others. A parent who learns to calm themselves can comfort a scared child. A teacher who understands their own triggers can choose patience instead of anger. Over time, these small moments add up, creating ripples that can transform families, schools, and entire communities.
Of course, this work is slow, and it takes real courage. It means facing not just our own pain, but the pain of our ancestors—and sometimes, the pain of an entire nation. It means learning to sit with discomfort, to listen to what our bodies are really saying, and to believe—deep down—that healing is possible, even when the wounds run deep.
